papers.title_in_file: Comparing performance of variational quantum algorithm simulations on HPC systems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections V and VII (results) and VIII (discussion and conclusions); sections II to IV and VI skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A benchmarking study that ports VQE and QAOA problem definitions (H2, MaxCut, TSP) across several HPC systems and quantum circuit simulators.

assertions.value: The authors report that their Hamiltonian and ansatz parser toolchain translated a problem definition successfully between different simulators.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section VIII, p.1 and p.9
quotes: The results show that our toolchain can successfully translate a problem definition between different simulators.
The verification run in Section VII-C proved this approach successful
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a small set of use cases.

assertions.value: The authors report that the 20-qubit MaxCut instance shows promising scaling on one node but is already at the limit of what can be simulated usefully in time to solution, with a quantum state memory footprint of only 16 MB.
assertions.anchor: Section VIII Discussion and Conclusions, p.9
quotes: The 20-qubit instance of the problem presents a promising scaling on one node, however
this is already at the limit of what is possible to simulate usefully in terms of time to solution, and has a memory footprint of its quantum state of only 16 MB
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one node.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational algorithms are limited in scaling by long runtimes relative to their memory footprint, so they expose limited parallelism, and that job arrays only partially mitigate this.
quotes: variational algorithms are limited in their scaling by the long runtimes with respect to their memory footprint, so they expose limited parallelism to computation.
This shortcoming is partially mitigated by using techniques like job arrays.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical conclusion from simulations of three use cases.

assertions.value: The authors state that the MaxCut tests focused on a single HPC node, without MPI node-to-node communication.
quotes: These tests are focused on a single HPC node, without making use of MPI for node-to-node communication.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test scope in Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: Scaling statements in the paper apply to one node only.

papers.title_in_file: Unsupervised Random Quantum Networks for PDEs
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 4 numerical results (Heat and HJB parts), conclusion; section 3 proofs and appendices not read in full
papers.what_it_is: A physics-informed quantum neural network method using random parameterised quantum circuits to solve Poisson, Heat and HJB PDEs, with a complexity analysis and simulations.

assertions.value: The authors report that they develop a complexity analysis of the approach and show numerically that random quantum networks can outperform more traditional quantum networks as well as random classical networks.
quotes: On the theoretical side, we develop a complexity analysis of this approach, and show numerically that random quantum networks can outperform more traditional quantum networks as well as random classical networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, on simulated circuits.
assertions.reader_inference: The HJB result in the same paper is described by the authors as poor, so the claim holds for some of the three equations.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the Heat equation with d = 1 the quantum network had a lower average MSE than the average of the classical networks, and that the classical network with the same number of trainable parameters had an MSE an order of magnitude larger.
quotes: For d = 1, the quantum network has a lower average MSE than the average values for the classical networks. Specifically, the classical network with the same number of trainable parameters has an MSE an order of magnitude larger.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from five training runs of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum state simulation is performed using the Yao package for Julia.
quotes: The quantum state simulation is performed using the Yao package for Julia
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own simulation setup in Section 4.
assertions.reader_inference: Results come from classical simulation, not quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report relatively poor performance for both the quantum and classical random networks on the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, attribute it to hardware limitations, and state that the MSE during training did not plateau for any of the models.
quotes: We see relatively poor performance for both sets of random networks, which is due to hardware limitations.
the MSE during training did not plateau for any of the models
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from one study; the cause is the authors' attribution.

papers.title_in_file: Large-Scale Quantum Kernels for Hyperspectral Data Classification
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, contributions, parts of sections V and VI, conclusion; table values and kernel-analysis details only skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of fidelity quantum kernel SVMs on hyperspectral Earth observation data, using tensor-network and GPU simulation and comparing with classical baselines.

assertions.value: The authors report that on four 50-band splits from Indian Pines the quantum kernel model achieved 78.0 ± 6.2% accuracy on a binary task, against 72.0±5.0% for the standard radial basis function (RBF) kernel.
quotes: on four 50-band splits selected from Indian Pines, the quantum model achieved a 78.0 ± 6.2% accuracy for a binary classification task compared to 72.0±5.0% for the standard radial basis function (RBF) kernel
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on four small splits, with overlapping standard deviations.
assertions.reader_inference: The gap is about the size of one standard deviation, so the data do not show a clear advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that on five 75-band splits from the Methane Detection dataset the quantum approach yielded 58.5 ± 5.0% accuracy versus 55.1 ± 2.5% for the classical counterpart.
quotes: On five 75-band splits selected from the Methane Detection dataset, the quantum approach yielded 58.5 ± 5.0% accuracy versus 55.1 ± 2.5% for the classical counterpart.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on five small splits.
assertions.reader_inference: Table IV in the same paper lists logistic regression at 0.587 accuracy against 0.585 for the quantum kernel SVM, so the quantum model is not best among all baselines on this task. The table figures are not in the quotes above.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum kernels were simulated using tensor network contraction techniques and GPU acceleration.
quotes: By simulating quantum kernels using tensor network contraction techniques and GPU acceleration
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own method in the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: Results are simulations, not runs on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the fact these fidelity kernels can be simulated classically undermines their potential to deliver a robust quantum advantage, while other constructions such as projected quantum kernels remain classically intractable.
quotes: the fact that these kernels can be simulated classically undermines their potential to deliver a robust quantum advantage.
other quantum kernel constructions, such as projected quantum kernels [9], remain classically intractable
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own approach in Section I.

papers.title_in_file: Molecular docking via quantum approximate optimization algorithm
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated 16 May 2024; record id says 2024, file name says 2023.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section III numerical simulation (8-qubit and 12-qubit parts), conclusion; methods and appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A method that maps molecular docking to a maximum vertex weight clique problem and solves it with QAOA and digitized-counterdiabatic QAOA in numerical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the 8-qubit docking example DC-QAOA reaches its optimal efficacy at p = 8 layers with 200 single-qubit and 80 two-qubit parametric gates, while conventional QAOA peaks at p = 24 with 392 single-qubit and 240 two-qubit parametric gates.
quotes: At p = 8 layers, DC-QAOA reaches its optimal efficacy, employing only 200 single-qubit and 80 two-qubit parametric gates. Conversely, conventional QAOA attains its peak performance at a significantly higher layer of p = 24, necessitating 392 single-qubit and 240 two-qubit parametric gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulation of one docking example.
assertions.reader_inference: The 8-qubit size comes from the paper's section text; the quote holds the gate counts.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the 12-qubit docking example, over 500 distinct sets of initial parameters, DC-QAOA achieved an accuracy (success) rate of 51% versus 32% for conventional QAOA.
quotes: we investigate the utilization of the QAOA-based molecular-docking algorithm in expanded quantum systems of 12 qubits.
We conducted a thorough evaluation of both the DCQAOA and the QAOA by subjecting them to simulations across 500 distinct sets of initial parameters.
the DC-QAOA algorithm achieved a noteworthy accuracy rate of 51%, whereas the conventional QAOA algorithm exhibited a considerably lower success rate of 32%
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from noise-free simulation of one 12-qubit example.
assertions.reader_inference: Both success rates are low in absolute terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that their investigation of a 12-qubit system with the QAOA-based algorithm encountered substantial challenges, and that the approach is vulnerable to converging towards local optima.
assertions.anchor: Section III end and Section IV Conclusion, p.11 to 12
quotes: Notwithstanding the promising outcomes achieved, our investigation into a 12-qubit system with the QAOAbased algorithm has encountered substantial challenges.
Nevertheless, one notable caveat of our approach is the algorithm's vulnerability to converging towards local optima within the vast parameter space.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in the Section IV conclusion and the end of Section III.
assertions.reader_inference: The study covers 6, 8 and 12 qubits only.

papers.title_in_file: Challenges in Applying Variational Quantum Algorithms to Dynamic Satellite Network Routing
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections 4.4, 6 (results), 7 (discussion) and 8 (conclusion); sections 2 and 3 on formulation skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A negative-results study of VQE, QAOA and a policy-gradient quantum reinforcement learning agent on satellite network routing, run on an ideal noise-free simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report that static optimizers (VQE and QAOA) were unable to solve a classically easy 4-node shortest path problem, which they attribute to the complexity of the optimization landscape.
quotes: Specifically, static optimizers are unable to solve even a classically easy 4-node shortest path problem due to the complexity of the optimization landscape.
assertions.certainty_reason: Negative empirical result from one study with a generic ansatz in noise-free simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The failure may reflect the N^2-qubit encoding and generic ansatz chosen, not VQAs in general.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the 5-node Max-Cut problem the QAOA implementation identified the optimal node partition, with an approximation ratio of 1.0.
quotes: For the 5-node Max-Cut problem, the QAOA implementation successfully identified the optimal node partition, achieving an approximation ratio of 1.0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one small canonical benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report that a basic QRL agent based on policy gradient methods failed to learn a useful routing strategy in a dynamic 8-node environment and performed no better than random actions, despite training over 3000 episodes.
quotes: Likewise, a basic QRL agent based on policy gradient methods fails to learn a useful routing strategy in a dynamic 8-node environment and performs no better than random actions.
Despite extensive training over 3000 episodes and substantial hyperparameter tuning
assertions.certainty_reason: Negative empirical result from one study with a vanilla REINFORCE agent.

assertions.value: The authors state that all experiments were conducted on a classical computer simulating an ideal, noise-free quantum processor.
quotes: All experiments were conducted on a classical computer simulating an ideal, noise-free quantum processor.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section 4.4.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware or noisy runs back the findings.

papers.title_in_file: A Grover-search Based Quantum Learning Scheme for Classification
papers.version_note: File is arXiv 1809.06056v2 dated 30 May 2022 (file name says 2018-09).
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, contributions, Theorem 2 statement, query complexity section, discussion and conclusion; proofs in appendices not read
papers.what_it_is: A Grover-search based learning scheme (GBLS) for quantum classifiers that cuts measurement counts and claims a query-complexity advantage on a specific binary classification task.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 2) that for GBLS under the optimal setting, the probability of sampling the outcome i∗ = K − 1 approaches 1 asymptotically iff the label of the last entry of Dk is yk = 1.
assertions.anchor: Section 2, Theorem 2, proof in Appendix A
quotes: Theorem 2 For GBLS, under the optimal setting, the probability of sampling the outcome i∗ = K − 1 approaches 1 asymptotically iff the label of the last entry of Dk is yk = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2, with proof in Appendix A (proof not read by this reader).

assertions.value: The authors state that the query complexity can be quadratically reduced over classical counterparts in the optimal setting (Theorem 2) for specific binary classification tasks, and that both classical algorithms and previous quantum classifiers need at least O(K) query complexity
quotes: the query complexity can be quadratically reduced over its classical counterparts in the optimal setting (see Theorem 2) when it is applied to accomplish specific binary classification tasks
both classical algorithms and previous quantum classifiers need at least O(K) query complexity
assertions.certainty_reason: The classical lower bound is stated, not proved, in the text read; the task is a constructed search-style task.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage holds for a search-structured classification task, not for classification in general. The authors call it a potential quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical simulations show GBLS achieves comparable performance with other quantum classifiers under various noise settings, while the required number of measurements is dramatically reduced.
quotes: Numerical simulations exhibit that GBLS can achieve comparable performance with other quantum classifiers under various noise settings, while the required number of measurements is dramatically reduced.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulations on a synthetic dataset in one study.

papers.title_in_file: ShadowNet for Data-Centric Quantum System Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and contributions, parts of section 4 results (TFIM/XXZ tables, noise-feature test), discussion and outlook; theory appendices not read
papers.what_it_is: A neural-network framework that trains on classical-shadow-derived datasets for quantum state tomography and direct fidelity estimation, evaluated by numerical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that in direct fidelity estimation for 60-qubit noisy GHZ states, ShadowNet achieves near-perfect estimation using just 200 training examples.
quotes: In the realm of direct fidelity estimation for 60-qubit noisy GHZ states, ShadowNet achieves near-perfect estimation using just 200 training examples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from numerical simulation in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Results are numerical simulations, per the abstract, not hardware runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that ShadowNet outperforms classical shadows with sufficient training data, 0.044 versus 0.477 when n = 800 and M = 500.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, TFIM and XXZ results, Table 1, p.11
quotes: ShadowNet dramatically outperforms classical shadows with sufficient training data, i.e., 0.044 versus 0.477 when n = 800 and M = 500.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulation of spin-model ground states in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote does not name the metric; it is read from the surrounding discussion of estimation error and should be checked against Table 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that insufficient training examples may incur overfitting and unsatisfactory performance of ShadowNet at the inference stage.
quotes: Insufficient training examples may incur overfitting and unsatisfactory performance of ShadowNet at the inference stage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from simulations in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: ShadowNet needs a training set of states from a similar class, a cost classical shadows do not carry.

papers.title_in_file: Algebraic Geometry of Quantum Graphical Models
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, statements of Theorems 3.3, 3.7, 5.5 and 5.10 and Question 3.12; proofs and appendix not read in full
papers.what_it_is: A pure mathematics paper that associates algebraic varieties to quantum graphical models and proves a quantum analogue of Birch's Theorem.

assertions.value: The authors prove a quantum analogue of Birch's Theorem, which generalises Birch's Theorem to quantum exponential families that become toric after a linear change of coordinates.
quotes: prove a quantum analogue of Birch's Theorem
This result generalises Birch's Theorem [8, Prop. 2.1.5] to quantum exponential families that become toric after a linear change of coordinates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 5.10 with Remark 5.11, Section 5.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for any graph G with N vertices, GV(HG) is an independence model on N binary random variables after a linear change of coordinates.
quotes: For any graph G with N vertices, GV(HG) is an independence model on N binary random variables after a linear change of coordinates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 5.5, Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors pose as an open question whether the variety QG is irreducible for any tree G.
quotes: Is the variety QG irreducible for any tree G?
assertions.certainty_reason: Question 3.12, Section 3: the authors state this as open.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper has no direct use for machine learning claims; it bears on quantum information structure only.
